questions.stem:
Three bags, $A$, $B$ and $C$, each contain 1 red marble and some green marbles.

Bag $A$ contains 1 red marble and 9 green marbles only
Bag $B$ contains 1 red marble and 4 green marbles only
Bag $C$ contains 1 red marble and 2 green marbles only

Sasha selects at random one marble from bag $A$.
If he selects a red marble, he stops selecting.
If the marble is green, he continues by selecting at random one marble from bag $B$.
If he selects a red marble, he stops selecting.
If the marble is green, he continues by selecting at random one marble from bag $C$.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
(a) Draw a tree diagram to represent this information.
(2)
parts.mark_scheme:
(a) B1: for correct shape (3 pairs) and at least one label on at least two pairs G(reen) and R(ed) allow G and G' or R and R' as labels, etc. condone 'extra' pairs if they are labelled with a probability of 0
dB1: (dep on previous B1) all correct i.e. for all 6 correct probabilities on the correct branches with at least one label on each pair
Official notes (completeness pass):
- (Whole question) Allow decimals or percentages throughout this question.

parts.label: b
parts.text:
(b) Find the probability that Sasha selects 3 green marbles.
(2)
parts.mark_scheme:
(b) $\frac{9}{10} \times \frac{4}{5} \times \frac{2}{3}$
M1: Multiplication of 3 correct probabilities (allow ft from their tree diagram)
$= \frac{12}{25}\ (= 0.48)$
A1: $\frac{12}{25}$ oe

parts.label: c
parts.text:
(c) Find the probability that Sasha selects at least 1 marble of each colour.
(2)
parts.mark_scheme:
(c) $\frac{9}{10} \times \frac{1}{5} + \frac{9}{10} \times \frac{4}{5} \times \frac{1}{3}$ or $1 - \left(\frac{1}{10} + \frac{9}{10} \times \frac{4}{5} \times \frac{2}{3}\right)$
M1: Either addition of only two correct products (product of two probs + product of three probs) which may ft from their tree diagram, or for $1 - ('\frac{1}{10}' + '(b)')$
$= \frac{21}{50}\ (= 0.42)$
A1: $\frac{21}{50}$ oe

parts.label: d
parts.text:
(d) Given that Sasha selects a red marble, find the probability that he selects it from bag $B$.
(2)
parts.mark_scheme:
(d) $[\mathrm{P}(\text{Red from } B \mid \text{Red selected})] = \dfrac{\frac{9}{10} \times \frac{4}{5} \times \frac{1}{5}}{\frac{1}{10} + \frac{9}{10} \times \frac{4}{5} \times \frac{1}{5} + \frac{9}{10} \times \frac{4}{5} \times \frac{1}{3}}\left[ = \dfrac{\frac{9}{50}}{\frac{13}{25}} \right]$
M1: Correct ratio of probabilities or correct ft ratio of probabilities e.g. $\dfrac{'\frac{9}{10}'\times'\frac{1}{5}'}{1-'(b)'}$ or $\dfrac{'\frac{9}{10}'\times'\frac{1}{5}'}{'\frac{1}{10}'+'(c)'}$ with num < den
$= \frac{9}{26}$
A1: $\frac{9}{26}$ (allow awrt 0.346)
Official notes (completeness pass):
- $[\mathrm{P}(\text{Red from } B \mid \text{Red selected})] = \dfrac{\frac{9}{10} \times \frac{1}{5}}{\frac{1}{10} + \frac{9}{10} \times \frac{1}{5} + \frac{9}{10} \times \frac{4}{5} \times \frac{1}{3}}\left[ = \dfrac{\frac{9}{50}}{\frac{13}{25}} \right]$

questions.stem:
The partially completed box plot in Figure 1 shows the distribution of daily mean air temperatures using the data from the large data set for Beijing in 2015

An outlier is defined as a value
more than $1.5 \times \mathrm{IQR}$ below $Q_1$ or
more than $1.5 \times \mathrm{IQR}$ above $Q_3$

The three lowest air temperatures in the data set are $7.6\,°\mathrm{C}$, $8.1\,°\mathrm{C}$ and $9.1\,°\mathrm{C}$
The highest air temperature in the data set is $32.5\,°\mathrm{C}$

parts.label: a
parts.text:
(a) Complete the box plot in Figure 1 showing clearly any outliers.
(4)
parts.mark_scheme:
(a) $\mathrm{IQR} = 26.6 - 19.4\ [= 7.2]$
B1: for a correct calculation for the IQR (implied by 10.8 or 8.6 or 37.4 seen)
$19.4 - 1.5 \times '7.2' [= 8.6]$ or $26.6 + 1.5 \times '7.2' [= 37.4]$
M1: for a complete method for either lower outlier limit or upper outlier limit (allow ft on their IQR) (may be implied by the 1st A1 or a lower whisker at 8.6)
Plotting one upper whisker to 32.5 and one lower whisker to 8.6 or 9.1
A1: both whiskers plotted correctly (allow $\frac{1}{2}$ square tolerance)
Plotting 7.6 and 8.1 as the only two outliers
A1: only two outliers plotted, 7.6 and 8.1 (must be disconnected from whisker)
NOTE: A fully correct box plot with no incorrect working scores 4/4

parts.label: b
parts.text:
(b) Using your knowledge of the large data set, suggest from which month the two outliers are likely to have come.
(1)
parts.mark_scheme:
(b) October (since it is the month with the coldest temperatures between May and October in Beijing)
B1
parts.notes: LDS convention (spec other_requirements: large data set)

parts.label: c
parts.text:
Using the data from the large data set, Simon produced the following summary statistics for the daily mean air temperature, $x\,°\mathrm{C}$, for Beijing in 2015

$n = 184 \qquad \sum x = 4153.6 \qquad S_{xx} = 4952.906$

(c) Show that, to 3 significant figures, the standard deviation is $5.19\,°\mathrm{C}$
(1)
parts.mark_scheme:
(c) $[\sigma =]\sqrt{\dfrac{4952.906}{184}}$ or e.g. $[\sigma =]\sqrt{\dfrac{S_{xx}}{n}} = 5.188...\ [=5.19*]$
B1cso*: Correct expression with square root or correct formula and 5.188 or better
Allow a complete correct method finding $\sum x^2 = \text{awrt } 98720$ and $\sigma = \sqrt{\dfrac{98715.9...}{184} - \left(\dfrac{4153.6}{184}\right)^2}$

parts.label: d
parts.text:
Simon decides to model the air temperatures with the random variable

$T \sim \mathrm{N}(22.6, 5.19^2)$

(d) Using Simon's model, calculate the 10th to 90th interpercentile range.
(3)
parts.mark_scheme:
(d) $z = (\pm)1.28(16)$ $[P_{90} =]29.251...$ or $[P_{10} =]15.948...$
B1: Identifying z-value for 10th or 90th percentile (allow awrt ($\pm$)1.28) or for identifying $[P_{90} =]29.251...$ (awrt 29.3) or $[P_{10} =]15.948...$ (awrt 15.9) (This may be implied by a correct answer awrt 13.3)
$2 \times 1.2816 \times 5.19$ '$29.251...$' $-$ '$15.948...$'
M1: for $2 \times z \times 5.19$ where $1 < z < 2$ or for their $P_{90} - P_{10}$ where $25 < P_{90} < 35$ and $10 < P_{10} < 20$
$= \text{awrt } 13.3$
A1: awrt 13.3

parts.label: e
parts.text:
Simon wants to model another variable from the large data set for Beijing using a normal distribution.

(e) State two variables from the large data set for Beijing that are **not** suitable to be modelled by a normal distribution. Give a reason for each answer.
(2)
parts.mark_scheme:
(e) Daily mean wind speed/Beaufort conversion since it is qualitative
B1
Rainfall since it is not symmetric/lots of days with 0 rainfall
B1
Allow any two of the following:
Wind speed/Beaufort since the data is non-numeric (o.e.). They need not mention Beaufort provided there is a description of the data as non-numeric (Do not allow wind direction/wind gust)
Rainfall as not symmetric/is skewed/is not bell shaped/lots of 0s/many days with no rain/mean$\neq$mode or median
Date since each data value appears once/it is uniformly distributed
Daily mean pressure since it is not symmetric/is skewed/not bell shaped
Daily mean wind speed since it is not symmetric/is skewed/not bell shaped
Do not allow 'not continuous' or 'discrete' as a supporting reason.
Ignore extraneous non-contradicting statements

- B1: for one variable identified and a correct supporting reason
B1: for two variables identified and a correct supporting reason for each

questions.stem:
Barbara is investigating the relationship between average income (GDP per capita), $x$ US dollars, and average annual carbon dioxide ($\mathrm{CO_2}$) emissions, $y$ tonnes, for different countries.

She takes a random sample of 24 countries and finds the product moment correlation coefficient between average annual $\mathrm{CO_2}$ emissions and average income to be 0.446

parts.label: a
parts.text:
(a) Stating your hypotheses clearly, test, at the 5% level of significance, whether or not the product moment correlation coefficient for all countries is greater than zero.
(3)
parts.mark_scheme:
(a) $\mathrm{H_0}: \rho = 0 \qquad \mathrm{H_1}: \rho > 0$
B1: for both hypotheses correct in terms of $\rho$
Critical value 0.3438
M1: for the critical value: sight of 0.3438 or any cv such that $0.25 < |\mathrm{cv}| < 0.45$
$(0.446 > 0.3438)$ so there is evidence that the product moment correlation coefficient (pmcc) is greater than 0/there is positive correlation
A1: a comment suggesting a significant result/ $\mathrm{H_0}$ is rejected on the basis of seeing $+0.3438$ and which mentions "pmcc/correlation/relationship" and "greater than 0/positive" (not just $\rho > 0$) or an answer in context e.g. 'as income'(o.e.) increases, '$\mathrm{CO_2}$/emissions'(o.e.) increases' A contradictory statement scores A0 e.g. 'Accept $\mathrm{H_0}$, therefore positive correlation'

parts.label: b
parts.text:
Barbara believes that a non-linear model would be a better fit to the data.
She codes the data using the coding $m = \log_{10} x$ and $c = \log_{10} y$ and obtains the model $c = -1.82 + 0.89m$

The product moment correlation coefficient between $c$ and $m$ is found to be 0.882

(b) Explain how this value supports Barbara's belief.
(1)
parts.mark_scheme:
(b) The value is close(r) to 1 or there is strong(er) (positive) correlation
B1: for suitable reason e.g. r is close(r) to 1 or "strong(er)"/"near perfect" correlation
Do not allow "association"

parts.label: c
parts.text:
(c) Show that the relationship between $y$ and $x$ can be written in the form $y = ax^n$ where $a$ and $n$ are constants to be found.
(5)
parts.mark_scheme:
(c) Method 1 (working to the model): $\log_{10} y = -1.82 + 0.89(\log_{10} x)$
M1: Correct substitution for both $c$ and $m$ (may be implied by 2nd M1 mark)
$y = 10^{-1.82 + 0.89(\log_{10} x)}$
M1: Making $y$ the subject to give an equation in the form $y = 10^{a+b(\log_{10} x)}$ (may be implied by 3rd M1 mark)
$y = 10^{-1.82} \times 10^{0.89(\log_{10} x)}\ [= 10^{-1.82} \times 10^{(\log_{10} x)^{0.89}}]$
M1: Correct multiplication to give an equation in the form $y = 10^a \times 10^{b(\log_{10} x)}$ (this line implies M1M1M1 provided no previous incorrect working seen)
$y = 0.015x^{0.89}$
A1A1

Method 2 (working from the model): $y = ax^n \rightarrow \log_{10} y = \log_{10}(ax^n)$
M1: Taking the log of both sides (may be implied by 2nd M1 mark)
$\log_{10} y = \log_{10} a + \log_{10} x^n$
M1: Correct use of the addition rule (may be implied by 3rd M1 mark)
$\log_{10} y = \log_{10} a + n\log_{10} x\ [\log_{10} a = -1.82, n = 0.89]$
M1: Correct multiplication of power (this line implies M1M1M1 provided no previous incorrect working seen)
$y = 0.015x^{0.89}$
A1A1

Notes: For both methods, once an M0 is scored, no further marks can be awarded and condone missing base 10 throughout
A1: $n = 0.89$ or $a = \text{awrt } 0.015$ or $y = ax^{0.89}$ or $y = \text{awrt } 0.015x^n$ (dep on M3)
A1: $n = 0.89$ and $a = \text{awrt } 0.015$ / $y = \text{awrt } 0.015x^{0.89}$ (dep on M3)
do not award the final A1 if answer is given in an incorrect form e.g. $y = 0.015 + x^{0.89}$

questions.stem:
Magali is studying the mean total cloud cover, in oktas, for Leuchars in 1987 using data from the large data set. The daily mean total cloud cover for all 184 days from the large data set is summarised in the table below.

$\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|}\hline \text{Daily mean total cloud cover (oktas)} & 0 & 1 & 2 & 3 & 4 & 5 & 6 & 7 & 8\\ \hline \text{Frequency (number of days)} & 0 & 1 & 4 & 7 & 10 & 30 & 52 & 52 & 28\\ \hline\end{array}$

One of the 184 days is selected at random.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
(a) Find the probability that it has a daily mean total cloud cover of 6 or greater.
(1)
parts.mark_scheme:
(a) $\dfrac{132}{184} = 0.71739...$ awrt 0.717
B1: Allow equivalent fraction, e.g. $\frac{33}{46}$
Official notes (completeness pass):
- (Whole question) Allow fractions, decimals or percentages throughout this question.

parts.label: b(i)
parts.text:
Magali is investigating whether the daily mean total cloud cover can be modelled using a binomial distribution.

She uses the random variable $X$ to denote the daily mean total cloud cover and believes that $X \sim \mathrm{B}(8, 0.76)$

Using Magali's model,

(b) (i) find $\mathrm{P}(X \geqslant 6)$
(2)
parts.mark_scheme:
(b)(i) $\mathrm{P}(X \geqslant 6) = 1 - \mathrm{P}(X \leqslant 5)$ or $\mathrm{P}([X=]6) + \mathrm{P}([X=]7) + \mathrm{P}([X=]8)$
M1: for writing or using $1 - \mathrm{P}(X \leqslant 5)$ or $\mathrm{P}(X=6) + \mathrm{P}(X=7) + \mathrm{P}(X=8)$
$= 1 - 0.296722... = \text{awrt } 0.703$
A1: awrt 0.703 (correct answer scores 2 out of 2)

parts.label: b(ii)
parts.text:
(ii) find, to 1 decimal place, the expected number of days in a sample of 184 days with a daily mean total cloud cover of 7
(2)
parts.mark_scheme:

questions.stem:
A machine puts liquid into bottles of perfume. The amount of liquid put into each bottle, $D\,\mathrm{ml}$, follows a normal distribution with mean $25\,\mathrm{ml}$

Given that 15% of bottles contain less than $24.63\,\mathrm{ml}$

parts.label: a
parts.text:
(a) find, to 2 decimal places, the value of $k$ such that $\mathrm{P}(24.63 < D < k) = 0.45$
(5)
parts.mark_scheme:
(a) $\dfrac{24.63-25}{'\sigma'} = -1.0364$
M1: for standardising 24.63, 25 and '$\sigma$' (ignore label) and setting = to $z$ where $1 < |z| < 2$
$[\sigma =]0.357$ (must come from compatible signs)
A1: $[\sigma =]$ awrt 0.36. Do not award this mark if signs are not compatible.
$\mathrm{P}(D>k) = 0.4$ or $\mathrm{P}(D<k) = 0.6$
B1: for either correct probability statement (may be implied by correct answer) this mark may be scored for a correct region shown on a diagram
$\dfrac{k-25}{'0.357'} = 0.2533$
M1: for a correct expression with $z = $ awrt 0.253 (may be implied by correct answer)
$k = \text{awrt } 25.09$
A1: awrt 25.09 (Correct answer with no incorrect working scores 5 out of 5)

parts.label: b
parts.text:
A random sample of 200 bottles is taken.

(b) Using a normal approximation, find the probability that fewer than half of these bottles contain between $24.63\,\mathrm{ml}$ and $k\,\mathrm{ml}$
(3)
parts.mark_scheme:
(b) $[Y \sim \mathrm{B}(200, 0.45) \rightarrow] W \sim \mathrm{N}(90, 49.5)$
B1: setting up normal distribution approximation of binomial N(90, 49.5) (may be implied by a correct answer) Look out for e.g. $\sigma = \frac{3\sqrt{22}}{2}$ or $\sigma = \text{awrt } 7.04$
$\mathrm{P}(Y<100) \approx \mathrm{P}(W<99.5)\left[=\mathrm{P}\left(Z < \dfrac{99.5-90}{\sqrt{49.5}}\right)\right]$
M1: attempting a probability using a continuity correction i.e. $\mathrm{P}(W<100.5)$, $\mathrm{P}(W<99.5)$ or $\mathrm{P}(W<98.5)$ condone $\leqslant$ (The continuity correction may be seen in a standardisation)
$= 0.9115...$ awrt 0.912
A1: awrt 0.912 [Note: 0.911299... from binomial scores 0 out of 3]

parts.label: c
parts.text:
The machine is adjusted so that the standard deviation of the liquid put in the bottles is now $0.16\,\mathrm{ml}$

Following the adjustments, Hannah believes that the mean amount of liquid put in each bottle is less than $25\,\mathrm{ml}$

She takes a random sample of 20 bottles and finds the mean amount of liquid to be $24.94\,\mathrm{ml}$

(c) Test Hannah's belief at the 5% level of significance. You should state your hypotheses clearly.
(5)
parts.mark_scheme:
(c) $\mathrm{H_0}: \mu = 25 \qquad \mathrm{H_1}: \mu < 25$
B1: for both hypotheses in terms of $\mu$
$[\bar{D} \sim]\ \mathrm{N}\left(25, \dfrac{0.16^2}{20}\right)$
M1: selecting suitable model must see N(normal), mean 25, sd $= \dfrac{0.16}{\sqrt{20}}$ (o.e.) or var $= \dfrac{4}{3125}$ (o.e.) Condone $\mathrm{N}\left(25, \dfrac{0.16}{\sqrt{20}}\right)$ if then used as s.d.
$\mathrm{P}(\bar{D}<24.94)[=\mathrm{P}(Z<-1.677...)] = 0.046766...$
A1: p value = awrt 0.047 or test statistic awrt $-1.68$ or CV awrt 24.941 (any of these values imply the M1 provided they do not come from Normal mean = 24.94)
$p = 0.047 < 0.05$ or $z = -1.677... < -1.6449$ or $24.94 < 24.94115...$ or reject $\mathrm{H_0}$/in the critical region/significant
M1: a correct comparison (including compatible signs) or correct non-contextual conclusion (f.t. their p value, test statistic or critical value in the comparison) M1 may be implied by a correct contextual statement NB Any contradictory non contextual statements/comparisons score M0A0 e.g. 'p < 0.05, not significant'
There is sufficient evidence to support Hannah's belief.
A1: correct conclusion in context mentioning Hannah's belief or the mean amount/liquid in each bottle is now less than 25ml (dep on M1A1M1)
